## 1. Verse-by-verse notes (the traditional reading)

**The whole psalm**
- The first letters of the verses follow the Hebrew alphabet, though not perfectly (an acrostic). Spurgeon thinks this may have been a memory aid as well as a poetic device. (Spurgeon PDF)
- Spurgeon finds it like Proverbs: short, pithy sayings. It has no prayer and doesn't mention David's own troubles. He reads it as the practical wisdom of an older man, like a church elder or a father speaking to his household. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible; Spurgeon PDF)
- The Expositor's Bible says not to expect the thought to move forward much in an acrostic psalm: the same ideas come back again and again. It also says the psalmist's answer to why the righteous suffer is only temporary, because the Cross was needed to explain that fully. Even so, his faith that sin is loss and righteousness is gain is "eternally true." (Expositor's)
- Guzik: David's answer to worry is not to deny the problem but to change perspective. The wicked's success is short, and God's care for the righteous is eternal. (Guzik)

**v. 1**
- The Hebrew word for "fret" literally means "get heated" or get worked up. Asaph wrestled with the same problem in Psalm 73. Guzik's picture: a wicked man's lavish dinner looks enviable until you learn it is his last meal on death row. (Guzik)
- Spurgeon says it is common for believers in hard times to feel badly treated when dishonest, irreligious people prosper. "To fret" means to worry, to have heartburn, to fume. (Spurgeon, StudyLight)
- Precept Austin notes the same Hebrew root is used of kindling anger (Job 19:11) and of working with burning zeal (Neh. 3:20). (Precept Austin)

**v. 2**
- The psalm keeps comparing the wicked to grass, green trees and smoke. These look healthy but fade quickly, so envying them is absurd. (Guzik)

**v. 3**
- Instead of envying, simply trust God and do good. Looking at the wicked's success easily distracts us from that simple work. (Guzik)
- "Dwell in the land": enjoy the blessings God gives. His faithfulness was like daily food to Israel. Guzik's translation reads "feed on His faithfulness." (Guzik)

**v. 4**
- Guzik's translation reads "Delight yourself *also* in the LORD." He says the "also" admits there are rightful joys outside the spiritual life. (Guzik)
- On "the desires of your heart," he says a person who truly delights in the Lord finds their desires changed until they match God's desires for them. Delight in God is the key to a satisfied life. (Guzik)
- Precept Austin gives practical ways to delight in God: read what He says about Himself, think it over prayerfully, trust His love, walk with Him, and hand everything over to Him. It also includes a devotional point: when our desires match God's will, we stop wanting things that can't satisfy, and real joy is wanting to be close to God. (Precept Austin)
- Spurgeon links three verses: in v. 4 we delight in the Lord, in v. 23 He delights in our way, and in v. 34 we keep His way. (Spurgeon PDF)

**v. 5**
- This verse explains what delighting in the Lord means: committing your way to Him and truly trusting Him, with a surrendered focus on God. (Guzik)

**v. 7**
- "Rest" (BSB "be still") means the rest of silence: not arguing in your own defence, and trusting God to protect you. (Guzik)
- The Expositor's Bible says this stillness is not inactivity. Patience here means eager, stretched-out expectation, not just putting up with things without complaining. (Expositor's)
- Older writers quoted by Spurgeon make several points. Resting in God means telling Him your griefs and letting Him choose for you. This promise covers trials God sends, not troubles we make for ourselves. Small daily irritations test us as much as big trials do. It is a real test of patience when God waits before acting against the wicked. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 8**
- Anger, wrath and fretting achieve nothing except harm. They are the opposite of delighting in God and waiting for Him. (Guzik)

**v. 9**
- God promises to care for His own both in this world and in the world to come. Evildoers will be cut off. (Guzik)
- Precept Austin: for now it can look as if Christians are losing, but those who wait on the Lord will inherit. (Precept Austin)

**v. 10**
- The wicked's success is short. People who are famous and praised now will soon have no standing at all. (Guzik)

**v. 11**
- Guzik quotes two definitions of "the meek." Horne: people who bear hardship, and their enemies' success, without envy, anger or complaint. Kidner: people who choose patient faith over pushing themselves forward. (Guzik)

**vv. 12–13**
- The wicked plot against the righteous for no reason. God laughs because He knows how it will end for them. (Guzik)

**vv. 14–15**
- The wicked don't stop at plotting; they act. Yet their own sword turns on them. (Guzik)
- Spurgeon: "Malice outwits itself." It drinks the poison it mixed for someone else. The wicked are busy ruining themselves while they think they are harming God's people. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 16**
- In its notes on the psalm, Precept Austin challenges the idea that a rich ungodly person deserves more honour than a poor godly one. In the end the ungodly person's life will hold nothing of lasting value. (Precept Austin)

**v. 17**
- The wicked have their arms broken; the righteous are held up by God's own arms. (Guzik)

**v. 18**
- The wicked's reward is passing; the inheritance of the upright is eternal. (Guzik)
- Spurgeon draws comfort from God's knowing His people and from how long their portion lasts. He calls it "entailed": legally secured so it can't be lost. (Spurgeon, StudyLight; Spurgeon PDF)
- Barnes: they will have a secure inheritance on earth that lasts into eternity in another world. (Barnes)
- Precept Austin quotes the NET translation: "The LORD watches over the innocent day by day." (Precept Austin)

**v. 19**
- God can provide for His own even when others have nothing. (Guzik)

**v. 20**
- The wicked's fame and success are like smoke, with no real substance. (Guzik)
- Barnes: the main meaning is probably that their crimes cut their lives short. But the word could also mean destruction in the next world. (Barnes)

**v. 21**
- The wicked are "takers." The difference between wicked and righteous shows in how they live, not only in what they believe. (Guzik)
- A different reading, from Daniel Cresswell (quoted by Spurgeon): "does not repay" may mean the wicked person *cannot* repay because he has become poor (compare Deut. 28:12). A Jew in that position became his creditor's slave (2 Kings 4:1). (Spurgeon, StudyLight)

**v. 22**
- This is the third time the psalm promises the inheritance. The blessed inherit; those cursed by the Lord are cut off. (Guzik)

**v. 23**
- See v. 4: here the Lord delights in our way. (Spurgeon PDF)

**v. 24**
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says the believer may fall through faint-heartedness but will not be cast off completely or for ever (2 Cor. 4:9). God's hand keeps him from falling away entirely. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 25**
- Guzik reads this as David's personal testimony over a long life, not a rule with no exceptions. Wisdom literature often states general truths in absolute terms. (Guzik)
- Precept Austin: a reminder for older believers tempted to doubt God. His faithfulness will be shown in the end, in eternity. (Precept Austin)
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon: under the Old Testament, earthly blessings like long life and children were more visible. But God still cares for His people's children, and serving God is still the surest way to establish a family. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 26**
- Spurgeon: the good man is a giver, not a borrower. He gives where there is real need, not to encourage idleness, and grows richer rather than poorer by giving. The text suggests it is usually better to give than to lend. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 27**
- Leave sin the way Lot left Sodom, without looking back. Make no deals with it. Whoever neglects to do good soon falls into evil. (Spurgeon, StudyLight)
- Precept Austin: the order matters, since you must turn from evil before you can do good. Truly good works depend on the Holy Spirit. "So you will abide forever" should not be read as earning eternal life by good works. (Precept Austin)
- The Expositor's Bible: the command "dwell for evermore" works as a promise of what will happen. (Expositor's)

**v. 28**
- God loves justice, so His people should too. He does not abandon His saints. (Guzik)

**v. 29**
- Spurgeon: the same promise is repeated in vv. 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34 for emphasis, and the word ("land" or "earth") should be translated the same way every time. (Spurgeon, StudyLight)

**v. 30**
- "Righteousness is wisdom in action," so a good man's speech is wise. He stands up for justice, judges people and things honestly, and warns that God's judgments will come. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible)

**v. 31**
- God's law in the heart is the foundation of everything lasting. Wise words and steady actions come from it, especially steady progress in right living. (Expositor's)

**v. 34**
- Spurgeon (via Precept Austin): the believer will have every earthly good that is truly good, and no limit of heavenly good. (Precept Austin)
- Spurgeon also urges endurance ("On, on, on"), linking it to "he that endureth to the end shall be saved." (Spurgeon PDF)

**vv. 35–36**
- The picture of the "well-rooted tree" fits the psalm's repeated image of things that look healthy but quickly fade. (Guzik)

**v. 37**
- Spurgeon's text (KJV) reads "Mark the perfect man... the end of that man is peace." Good men are worth studying; the man of peace has a peaceful end. (Spurgeon PDF)
- Barnes: the point is how each life ends, ruin for one and peace for the other, and the word can cover the whole future. (Barnes)
- Note that the BSB's "posterity awaits" is a different translation of this line. Barnes' notes don't discuss it.

**v. 38**
- The wicked's time, happiness and hopes are cut short. They have "no future worth having." (Spurgeon PDF)

**v. 39**
- "Sound doctrine this. The very marrow of the gospel of free grace": salvation comes from the Lord, not from the righteous themselves. (Spurgeon PDF)

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no sources putting traditions side by side on this psalm. Two points touch on doctrine, but I could only read one side of each:
- **v. 24 (and the psalm as a whole):** An older writer quoted by Spurgeon reads v. 24 as saying a believer may fall but is never completely cast off. Another quotation says the righteous are "preserved in Christ" and points to vv. 3, 17, 23, 25 and 32. This is the Reformed and Baptist teaching that true believers persevere to the end. (Spurgeon, Blue Letter Bible; Spurgeon PDF) I couldn't read Wesleyan or Lutheran sources on this verse, so I can't tell you whether they read it differently.
- **v. 27:** Precept Austin warns against reading "do good, so that you will abide forever" as earning salvation. Spurgeon's v. 39 note stresses "free grace." (Precept Austin; Spurgeon PDF)

## 3. Other views

I couldn't reach anything from modern scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox sources, or writing on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching about v. 4. The closest thing is Guzik's and Precept Austin's point on v. 4: God changes our desires rather than simply granting them. I can't say from what I read whether they meant this as a reply to prosperity teaching.
